meta.blurb: Follow a bored girl and a very late White Rabbit down a hole, into a world where cakes make you grow, cats vanish, and a Queen wants everyone's head. Lewis Carroll's dream is funny, strange and unforgettable.
meta.bible: Alice: a curious, polite seven-year-old girl in a blue dress who falls asleep on a riverbank. Her sister reads on the bank and wakes her at the end. Dinah: Alice's pet cat. The White Rabbit: a nervous rabbit in a waistcoat with a pocket watch, always late, who works for the Duchess and the Queen. Bill the Lizard: the Rabbit's servant, kicked out of the chimney. The Mouse: frightened of cats. The Dodo, a Duck, a Lory and an Eaglet: animals in the pool who run the Caucus-race. The Caterpillar: a blue Caterpillar on a mushroom, smokes a long pipe, asks Who are you. The mushroom: one side makes Alice grow, the other makes her shrink. The Pigeon: thinks Alice is a serpent. The Duchess: bad-tempered at first, kind later, finds a moral in everything. The Cook: throws pots and pans, uses too much pepper. The Cheshire Cat: grins, appears and vanishes, says we are all mad here. The Mad Hatter, the March Hare and the Dormouse: the Mad Tea-Party, always six o'clock because they quarrelled with Time. The Queen of Hearts: furious, shouts Off with her head. The King of Hearts: mild, hushes her. The Knave of Hearts: accused of stealing the Queen's tarts. The Gryphon and the Mock Turtle: the Mock Turtle's lessons are Reeling, Writhing, Ambition, Distraction, Uglification and Derision. The Lobster Quadrille. Rule Forty-two. Rule One. Wonderland: a dream world under the ground. Places: the riverbank, the rabbit hole, the hall of doors, the pool of tears, the little garden door, the Rabbit's house, the wood, the Duchess's kitchen, the Queen's croquet-ground, the courtroom. Objects: a tiny golden key, a bottle marked Drink me, a cake marked Eat me, the Rabbit's white gloves and fan, flamingo mallets, hedgehog balls. Voice and tone: warm, playful, curious; dream logic, wit and gentle humour. Nothing is truly frightening, and the ending is a waking, happy one.

B1B2: Alice is sitting on the riverbank beside her sister, who is reading a book with no drawings in it. Alice is so bored that she wonders whether making a daisy chain is worth the trouble.
Suddenly a White Rabbit in a waistcoat hurries past her, muttering that he is terribly late. What surprises Alice most is that he pulls a watch out of his pocket and looks at it.
Burning with curiosity, Alice dashes across the field after him and sees him vanish down a large rabbit hole. Without stopping to think how she will ever get out again, she jumps in after him.
The hole is so deep that Alice falls slowly, with time to look at the cupboards and shelves around her. She wonders where she will land, and she hopes that Dinah, her cat, will not miss her milk.
At last she lands on a heap of dry leaves, but the Rabbit has already rushed off down a passage. She finds herself in a long hall full of doors, and every single one of them is locked.

On a glass table she discovers a tiny golden key, and it fits a little door hidden behind a curtain. Through the door she can see a beautiful garden, but the opening is far too small for her to squeeze through.

Nearby stands a bottle labelled “Drink me,” and Alice, after checking that it is not marked poison, takes a small sip. To her amazement she begins to shrink until she is only ten inches tall, just the right size for the door.

Unfortunately, she has left the golden key on the glass table, and now it is much too high for her to reach. She tries to climb up one leg of the table, but it is too slippery, and she sits down and cries.
Under the table Alice finds a small cake with the words “Eat me” spelled out in currants. She nibbles it, and before long she is stretching upwards, so tall that her feet seem miles away.
Far too big for the door, Alice weeps so hard that a great pool of tears spreads across the floor. She scolds herself for crying, but the tears keep coming, and soon the water reaches her ankles.

The White Rabbit hurries back with white gloves and a fan, and he drops both when Alice speaks to him. Alice picks up the fan, and as she waves it she shrinks again and slips into the pool of her own tears.
Swimming about in the salt water, Alice meets a Mouse, and she tries to make friends by talking about her cat Dinah. The poor Mouse is so frightened by the mention of cats that it shivers all over.

The pool is soon crowded with birds and animals, and they all scramble ashore, wet and cross. The Dodo suggests a Caucus-race to dry everyone off, and the creatures run in a circle, starting and stopping whenever they please.
Nobody wins, or rather everybody does, so the Dodo declares that all must have prizes. Alice, who has a box of sweets in her pocket, shares them out, and she herself receives a thimble.

Left alone, Alice thinks sadly of Dinah until the White Rabbit trots back, looking for his lost gloves and fan. He mistakes her for his housemaid and orders her to go to his house and fetch them at once.

Alice finds the Rabbit's neat little house and goes upstairs, where she drinks from another bottle without reading the label. Almost at once she fills the room, with one arm out of the window and a foot up the chimney.
The Rabbit and Bill the Lizard try in vain to get in, and poor Bill is sent down the chimney. Alice gives a sharp kick, and Bill goes flying out of the chimney like a rocket.
The crowd outside throws pebbles through the window, and the pebbles turn into little cakes on the floor. Alice eats one, shrinks to a small size, and runs out of the house into a thick wood.
In the wood she finds a large blue Caterpillar sitting on a mushroom, smoking a long pipe. He looks at her for a long time before asking, in a slow, sleepy voice, “Who are you?”

Alice explains that she has changed size so often today that she hardly knows who she is. The Caterpillar tells her that one side of the mushroom will make her grow and the other will make her shrink.

She nibbles the wrong side first, and her neck stretches so far that an angry pigeon mistakes her for a serpent. More careful nibbling brings her back to her proper height, and she comes upon a tiny house in the wood.

Alice steps inside, where the kitchen is full of smoke and pepper, and everyone sneezes except the cook and a grinning cat. The Duchess nurses a howling baby on a stool while the cook throws pots and pans at everyone.
The Duchess hands Alice the baby and hurries off to play croquet with the Queen. Soon the baby's nose turns up, its eyes grow small, and in her arms it becomes a pig.
Alice sets the pig down, and it trots happily away into the trees. She decides that it would have made an ugly child, but it makes a rather handsome pig.

In a tree nearby sits the Cheshire Cat, grinning from ear to ear, and Alice politely asks which way she should go. The Cat replies that it depends on where she wants to go, and adds that everyone here is mad.
He explains that a Hatter lives in one direction and a March Hare in the other, and that both are mad. Then the Cat vanishes bit by bit, until only his wide grin hangs in the air.

Alice finds the March Hare and the Mad Hatter having tea at a large table, with a sleepy Dormouse squashed between them. They cry out that there is no room as she approaches, although the table is almost empty, and she sits down anyway.

The Hatter asks why a raven is like a writing desk, but nobody has an answer, not even the Hatter himself. He also complains that his watch tells the day of the month rather than the time, which seems perfectly sensible to him.
They explain that they have quarrelled with Time, so it is always six o'clock and tea is always ready. When the cups get dirty, they simply move along to the next clean place around the table.

Alice grows tired of the nonsense, and the Dormouse falls asleep in the middle of a story, so she walks away. Soon she finds a door in a tree, and with the key and some mushroom she steps into the lovely garden.
In the garden three gardeners are busily painting a rose tree red, because they planted white roses by mistake. They are terrified that the Queen of Hearts will find out and be furious.

A grand procession arrives, with soldiers, courtiers and royal children, followed by the White Rabbit, the King and the Queen of Hearts. Everyone throws themselves flat on the ground except Alice, who wonders what use a parade would be if everyone lay face down.

The Queen glares at Alice and turns purple with rage, and the King gently reminds her that Alice is only a child. Even so, the Queen stamps her foot and screams her favourite order, “Off with her head!”

The Queen invites Alice to a game of croquet, but the mallets are live flamingos and the balls are hedgehogs. The soldiers bend over to make the hoops, and nothing in this strange game ever stays still for a moment.

Then the Cheshire Cat's head appears in the air, and the royal couple argue about whether it can be removed. The Queen quarrels with every player and orders heads off right and left, which makes Alice nervous.
The Duchess, now surprisingly friendly, takes Alice's arm and finds a moral in everything they see. The Queen soon arrives with a frown, and the Duchess hurries away in fear for her head.
The Queen tells Alice to visit the Mock Turtle, and a sleepy Gryphon leads her to the seaside. They find the Mock Turtle sitting sadly on a rock, sighing as if his heart were about to break.
The Mock Turtle tells Alice that his school was under the sea, with lessons in Reeling, Writhing and Uglification. Alice thinks these lessons very peculiar, and she hides a smile behind her hand.

The Gryphon and the Mock Turtle dance the Lobster Quadrille, stepping solemnly along the shore while the Turtle sings. Alice watches with delight, though she is startled when a distant cry announces that the trial is beginning.

The King and Queen of Hearts sit on their thrones, surrounded by a crowd of birds, animals and playing cards. The Knave of Hearts stands in chains in front of them, accused of stealing the Queen's tarts.

The White Rabbit blows a trumpet and reads out a rhyme about how the Queen made some tarts and lost them. The King calls for the first witness while the twelve animals of the jury scribble on their slates.

The Hatter shuffles in, trembling, with a teacup in one hand and bread and butter in the other. He is so nervous that he bites a piece out of his teacup, and the King grows impatient with his rambling answers.

Meanwhile Alice feels a very odd sensation, and she realises she is slowly growing larger again. The Dormouse, sitting beside her, complains that she has no right to grow so fast and takes up too much room.
When Alice is called as a witness, she jumps up so fast that her skirt tips over the jury box. The little animals tumble out onto the crowd, and Alice anxiously puts them back one by one.
The King announces that anyone more than a mile high must leave the court. Alice replies that she is not nearly so tall, and that he has only just invented the rule.

The Rabbit produces a mysterious letter, and the King reads out some muddled verses that supposedly prove the Knave guilty. Alice declares that there is not an atom of sense in them, which makes the whole court gasp.
The Queen, ignoring all argument, insists that the sentence must come first and the verdict afterwards. Alice says this is nonsense, and the furious Queen orders the soldiers to seize her.
By now full size again, Alice shouts that nobody here frightens her, because they are nothing but a pack of cards. At that the whole pack rises into the air and comes flying down upon her.
She screams and tries to beat the cards away, and then she wakes on the riverbank, her head in her sister's lap. Her sister is gently brushing a few dead leaves from her face.

Alice tells her sister about her strange dream, and her sister listens with a smile before sending her in to tea. As she runs in, she thinks what a curious dream it was, and how lucky she is to have had it.
C1C2: Alice was beginning to tire of sitting idly on the riverbank beside her sister, who was absorbed in a book that offered neither drawings nor conversation. The afternoon was so hot and drowsy that the whole world seemed to have slowed to a murmur. She was weighing, with what little energy the heat had left her, whether the pleasure of making a daisy chain would justify the trouble of getting up to pick the daisies.

Quite suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes bolted past her, muttering in great agitation that he would be dreadfully late. There was little remarkable in that, or even in his muttering, until he drew a watch from his waistcoat pocket, consulted it gravely, and hurried on. Alice sprang to her feet, struck by the thought that she had never in her life met a rabbit who wore a waistcoat and carried a timepiece.

Burning with curiosity, she raced across the field in pursuit and was just in time to see him dart into an enormous rabbit hole beneath the hedge. In another moment she had plunged in after him, giving no thought whatever to how she might ever climb out again. The tunnel ran straight on like a passage for some distance, and then dipped so suddenly that she had no chance to stop herself.

Down she fell, and the shaft was so deep, or she fell so slowly, that she had ample leisure to gaze about her and wonder what would happen next. Cupboards and bookshelves lined the walls, and as she drifted past one she lifted a jar of marmalade, only to find it disappointingly empty. Her thoughts drifted to her cat Dinah, and she hoped that someone would remember the saucer of milk at teatime.

At length, with a soft thump, she landed on a heap of sticks and dry leaves, unhurt, and sprang up in time to glimpse the Rabbit hurrying down a long passage. She followed, but he turned a corner and was gone, leaving her alone in a low, long hall lit by a row of lamps hanging from the roof. Doors lined it on every side, yet when she tried them one by one, each proved to be locked, and she wandered sadly down the middle, wondering how she would ever get out.

Presently she came upon a little glass table, and on it lay nothing but a tiny golden key, which she tried hopefully in every lock. It was too small for any of the great doors, but on her second circuit she noticed a low curtain, and behind it a door scarcely fifteen inches high, which the key fitted perfectly. Beyond it lay a passage no wider than a rat-hole, and at its end shone the loveliest garden she had ever seen, bright with flowers and cool with fountains.

Alice longed to reach the garden, but she was far too large to fit through the doorway, and she wished she could somehow fold herself away. Beside the table, as though in answer, stood a little bottle that had certainly not been there before, and round its neck hung a paper label bearing the words “Drink me”. Prudent child that she was, Alice first checked that it was not marked poison, and only when she found it delicious did she drink it down and begin to dwindle.

Down she shrank until she stood scarcely ten inches high, and her face brightened at the thought that she was now exactly the right size for the little door. Alas, on reaching it she found that she had left the golden key upon the glass table, and she could see it plainly through the glass but could not possibly reach it. She tried to climb one of the table's legs, but it was far too slippery, and at last the poor child sat down and cried.

Presently she spotted a small glass box beneath the table, and in it a tiny cake with the words “Eat me” picked out in currants. Reasoning that growing would bring the key within reach, while shrinking would let her creep under the door, she nibbled a corner and waited. To her astonishment she began to stretch upward at a dizzying rate until her head struck the ceiling and her feet seemed to belong to somebody a mile away.

Now nine feet tall and quite unable to pass through the little door, Alice wept so copiously that a great pool formed around her and spread across half the hall. She scolded herself severely for such behaviour, telling herself that a girl of her size ought to be ashamed, and yet the tears kept falling. Presently she heard a patter of little feet in the distance, and she hastily dried her eyes, eager to see who was coming.

It was the White Rabbit, splendidly dressed and carrying a pair of white gloves and a large fan, muttering anxiously about the Duchess and her temper. When Alice timidly addressed him, he started violently, dropped both gloves and fan, and scurried off into the darkness. Alice picked up the fan, and as she cooled herself in the stuffy hall she noticed she was shrinking again, and dropped it only just in time to avoid vanishing altogether.

With a splash she tumbled into salt water up to her chin, and for a moment she supposed she had fallen into the sea, until she realised it was the pool of her own tears. Soon a mouse that had likewise slipped in came swimming by, and Alice, hoping to be friendly, chatted to it as politely as she could. This went badly, for when she mentioned her cat Dinah, the poor creature trembled from nose to tail, and Alice hurried to apologise.

Before long the pool was crowded with birds and beasts that had fallen in, among them a Duck, a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet, and the whole bedraggled company swam for the shore. They stood dripping on the bank, cross and uncomfortable, and debated gravely among themselves how best to get dry again. The Dodo, with the air of a scholar, proposed a Caucus-race, which proved to be a circular course where everybody started and stopped whenever they pleased.

Soon everyone was dry again, and the Dodo, after much solemn thought, announced that everybody had won and that all must have prizes. Alice, having no choice, handed round the sweets from her pocket, and each animal received one, while she herself was awarded her own thimble with great ceremony. Then they all ate their sweets, with a good deal of noise and confusion, and some of the birds choked and had to be patted on the back.

Left alone again, Alice fell to wondering sadly about home and her cat Dinah, until at length the White Rabbit came pattering back, searching anxiously for the gloves and fan he had lost. Catching sight of her, he mistook her for his housemaid and ordered her, in a tone of great irritation, to run to his house and fetch them at once. Alice was so startled that she obeyed without a word, running straight off in the direction he had pointed and not stopping to explain his mistake.

She soon found a neat little house with a shining brass plate bearing the Rabbit's name, and she hurried upstairs in fear of meeting the real housemaid and being turned out. Upstairs she found the fan, a pair of gloves, and, beside the mirror, a small bottle with no label, which she drank without a second thought. Almost at once she grew so enormous that her head pressed against the ceiling, one elbow jutted out of the window, and one foot was wedged up the chimney.

Outside, the indignant Rabbit tried in vain to open the door, which was jammed shut by Alice's elbow, and so he sent poor Bill the Lizard down the chimney. Alice waited until she heard a scratching and scrabbling just above her, then drew her foot as far down as it would go and gave a sudden kick. There was a cry and a distant crash as poor Bill shot out of the chimney like a rocket, to the great alarm of the crowd gathered outside.

A shower of pebbles rattled through the window, and to her surprise Alice saw that each one, as it struck the floor, was turning into a little cake. Reasoning that any cake she ate must change her size, and that she could hardly grow larger, she swallowed one and felt herself dwindle at once. As soon as she was small enough to fit through the door, she bolted out into a thick wood, pursued by a crowd of curious creatures.

Once in the wood she resolved to grow back to her proper size and to find a way into that lovely garden, though she had no idea how to achieve either. Her eye soon fell upon a large mushroom as tall as herself, and on top of it sat a blue Caterpillar, puffing at a long pipe, quite indifferent to the world. After a long, languid silence the creature took the pipe from its mouth and asked, in a drowsy voice, “Who are you?”

Alice replied rather shyly that she hardly knew, since she had changed size several times that day and felt quite muddled. The Caterpillar was unmoved and demanded a clearer account, which was precisely what Alice could not give, being no longer sure who she was. As she turned to leave, he called her back and told her that one side of the mushroom would make her grow taller and the other would make her shrink.

Unsure which side was which, since the mushroom was perfectly round, Alice broke off a piece with each hand, and the first nibble she tried made her chin strike her foot. The second sent her neck shooting up above the treetops like a stalk, where an indignant pigeon mistook her for a serpent and flew at her face, scolding furiously about eggs. By nibbling cautiously at each piece in turn she at last coaxed herself back to her proper height, and soon afterwards she came upon a small house in the middle of the wood.

Alice pushed open the door of the little house and stepped into a kitchen so thick with smoke and pepper that she could scarcely see across it. Everybody in the room was sneezing except for the cook, who stirred an enormous pot of soup, and a large cat that lay on the hearth grinning from ear to ear. In the middle of the room, on a three-legged stool, sat the Duchess, nursing a baby that howled and sneezed in turn, while the cook flung pots and pans at anyone within range.

The Duchess, who was in no mood for pleasantries, tossed the baby to Alice and hurried off to play croquet with the Queen, leaving the cook to hurl a frying pan after her. Alice carried the child out into the fresh air, where it grunted so oddly that she looked down and found its nose turned up and its eyes grown small. Before she could decide what to do, it had become, beyond any doubt, a pig, and she knew she could not carry such a creature any further.

She set it down, and it trotted off contentedly into the wood, and she watched it go with a feeling of relief. Alice reflected that, as a child, it would have grown up extremely ugly, though as a pig it was really rather handsome. Then she wondered which of her acquaintances would make good pigs, and had nearly decided that she knew several, when a sudden rustle made her look up.

There, on a bough of a nearby tree, sat the Cheshire Cat, grinning from ear to ear and displaying a great many teeth, which struck Alice as impolite but also rather friendly. She asked him, very politely, which way she ought to go from there, and he answered that it depended entirely on where she wanted to get to. Told that it hardly mattered, he remarked that any road would do, and added with perfect calm that everybody here was mad, herself included.

The Cat explained, with the patience of one addressing a slow pupil, that a Hatter lived in one direction and a March Hare in the other, and that both were mad. Alice chose to visit the Hare, but she had barely made up her mind when the Cat began to fade. First his tail vanished, then his body, and last of all his great grin, which lingered in the air long after the rest of him had gone.

The March Hare's house had a table laid for tea under a tree, and at it sat the Hare and the Hatter, with a sleepy Dormouse wedged between them as a cushion. The table was enormous, yet the three of them were crowded together at one corner and cried out that there was no room the moment they saw Alice approaching. She protested indignantly that there was plenty of room, and settled into a large armchair at the end of the table.

The Hatter, who had been staring at her with great curiosity, suddenly asked why a raven is like a writing desk, and Alice, delighted at the prospect of riddles, set about guessing. Nobody, it turned out, knew the answer, not even the Hatter himself, who confessed that he had merely thought of the question and had no idea what would solve it. Meanwhile he pulled out his watch, shook it, and complained that it told the day of the month rather than the hour, which Alice thought useless but he found quite natural.

They explained that they had quarrelled with Time, who now refused to oblige them, so that it was always six o'clock and always the hour for tea. Since there was never a chance to wash up, they simply moved along the table one place at a time whenever a setting grew too dirty to use. When Alice asked what happened when they came back to the beginning, the Hare changed the subject at once, and the Dormouse was woken for a story.

The Dormouse began a drowsy tale about three sisters in a well of treacle, but he kept falling asleep midway, and Alice rose in disgust and walked away. Behind her the Hatter and the Hare went on squabbling and did not even seem to notice that she had gone. In a nearby tree she spotted a door in the trunk, and with a nibble of mushroom and the golden key in her hand she stepped through into the lovely garden at last.

Beside a great rose tree near the entrance, three gardeners were busily painting the white roses red, having planted the wrong tree by mistake. They worked in a fever of anxiety, arguing over whose fault it was and begging one another to be quick. Their terror was easily explained, for they knew that if the Queen of Hearts discovered the error, she would fly into one of her famous rages.

Presently a splendid procession came into view, led by soldiers armed with clubs, followed by courtiers and royal children, and last of all the White Rabbit, the King and the Queen of Hearts. Everyone flung themselves flat upon the ground, but Alice, reflecting that a parade would be pointless if everybody lay down, remained standing and watched with interest. The royal pair paused before her, and the Queen, studying her with a fierce eye, drew herself up to her full height.

The Queen demanded to know who this child was, and Alice, whose boldness surprised even herself, replied that she was simply Alice. Purple with fury, the Queen glared at her like a wild beast and then screamed the order that had made her famous, “Off with her head!” The King, however, laid a timid hand on her arm and reminded her gently that Alice was only a child.

The Queen commanded Alice to join the croquet game, and a stranger match was never played, for the mallets were live flamingos, the balls were hedgehogs, and the hoops were bent soldiers. Alice found that her flamingo kept twisting its long neck round to look up at her with such puzzlement that she burst into laughter. Nothing stayed in place for an instant, for the hedgehogs unrolled and wandered off whenever they pleased, and every player quarrelled with the others at once.

Amid the uproar the Queen stamped about, ordering heads to be cut off right and left, until Alice began to look anxiously for a way to escape. Then a curious shimmer in the air resolved itself into a grin, and soon the whole head of the Cheshire Cat hung there without a body to keep it company. The King and Queen promptly fell to arguing over whether anything could be cut off that had no body, and the whole court waited to hear who would win.

The Duchess, now surprisingly affectionate, slipped an arm through Alice's and found a moral in everything they saw, however trivial or absurd. Alice, who would have preferred fewer morals and more elbow room, listened politely while wondering why the Duchess had changed so much. The Queen soon swept up with a thunderous frown and ordered the Duchess to be gone at once or lose her head, whereupon the Duchess vanished in an instant.

Weary of the game, the Queen sent Alice off to meet the Mock Turtle, and a Gryphon, lying fast asleep in the sun, was roused to take her there. The Gryphon led the way, chuckling as he assured her that the Queen's threats were all talk and nobody was ever really punished. At last they found the Mock Turtle sitting forlorn on a ledge of rock, and as they drew near they could hear him sighing as though his heart would break.

In a voice broken by sobs, the Mock Turtle told Alice that he had once been a real turtle and had attended school at the bottom of the sea. His lessons included Reeling and Writhing and the four branches of Arithmetic, namely Ambition, Distraction, Uglification and Derision. Alice, who had never heard of such subjects, found them so peculiar that she hid her smile behind her hand, for fear of hurting his feelings.

Having exhausted the subject of schooling, the Gryphon proposed that they dance the Lobster Quadrille for Alice, and the two rose with great solemnity. Forming a line along the sandy shore, they advanced and retreated, passed lobsters from partner to partner, and flung them far out to sea while the Mock Turtle sang mournfully. Alice watched with delight and even joined in for a few steps, until a distant cry announced that a trial was about to begin.

The Gryphon seized her hand and hurried her away, and when they arrived they found the King and Queen of Hearts seated upon their thrones, with a great crowd gathered round them. The Knave of Hearts stood before them in chains, with a soldier on each side, while the jury, a dozen assorted creatures, sat in a box beside them. The charge against the prisoner was that he had stolen the tarts which the Queen had baked with her own royal hands.

At a blast from the White Rabbit's trumpet the court fell silent, and he unrolled a parchment and read out a rhyme about the Queen, some tarts, and a theft. The King ordered the jury to consider their verdict, only to be corrected by the Rabbit, who reminded him that witnesses must come first. The jury meanwhile scribbled busily on their slates, and Alice noticed that they were writing down their own names for fear of forgetting them before the trial ended.

The first witness was the Hatter, who shuffled in trembling, with a teacup in one hand and a slice of bread and butter in the other. The King commanded him to give his evidence without being nervous, a command which frightened him so much that he bit a large piece out of his teacup instead of his bread. Whatever he said only deepened the confusion, and the King grew more impatient with every rambling answer until the poor fellow was told to stand down.

Meanwhile Alice felt a very odd sensation which puzzled her until she realised that she had begun to grow larger again, and she wondered whether she ought to leave the court altogether. The Dormouse, sitting beside her, protested that she had no business to grow at such a rate, since he could hardly breathe. Alice replied that she could not help it, and the Dormouse, with a grumble, got up and shifted to the far side of the court.

When the Hatter had been dismissed, the King called for the next witness, and the Rabbit, reading from his list, squeaked out the name of Alice. Alice jumped up in a flurry that made her forget how large she had grown, and the edge of her skirt swept the jury box and sent its occupants tumbling onto the crowd below. Dismayed, she gathered them up one by one and set them back in their seats, though Bill the Lizard went in upside down and sat gazing at the roof.

Quite undisturbed by the wreckage, the King announced that under Rule Forty-two every person more than a mile high must leave the court, and he looked pointedly at Alice. Alice protested that she was nowhere near so tall and that it was no regular rule at all but one he had invented only a moment before. The King, turning rather pink about the ears, claimed that it was the oldest rule in the book, and Alice replied sweetly that in that case it ought to be Rule One.

Then the White Rabbit produced a mysterious letter, supposedly written by the prisoner, though it was signed by nobody and addressed to nobody in particular. The King read out a set of muddled verses, convinced that they proved the Knave guilty, although they were so full of nonsense that no two lines agreed with each other. Alice, who had grown so tall that she no longer feared anyone, declared that there was not an atom of meaning in the whole poem, and the entire court gasped.

The Queen, who had listened with growing impatience, announced that the sentence must come first and the verdict afterwards. Alice declared that this was complete nonsense, and the Queen, turning purple, ordered the soldiers to seize her. The soldiers, however, hesitated, for Alice had grown to an enormous size, and not one of them wished to be the first to lay a hand on her.

Standing at her full height and no longer afraid of anyone, Alice cried that nobody there frightened her, for they were nothing but a pack of cards. At these words the whole pack rose into the air and came flying down upon her in a rustling storm. She gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and struck out wildly to beat them away.

In an instant the cards and the court were gone, and Alice lay on the riverbank with her head in her sister's lap, blinking in the warm sunlight. Her sister was gently brushing away a few dead leaves that had fluttered down onto her face from the trees above. Alice stretched and yawned, still feeling the strangeness of the dream hanging about her like a faint perfume, and sat up slowly.

Alice sat up and told her sister, as well as she could remember, about the strange adventures she had just had, from the White Rabbit to the Queen and her pack of cards. Her sister listened with a thoughtful smile, kissed her, and said it had been a curious dream, but now it was high time for tea. Alice ran in across the grass, thinking as she went, with a happy smile, what a wonderful dream it had been.
